viewer_sees: Athena leaping full-grown out of a blaze of white-gold light, spear shaken high, Zeus astonished on his throne at her back (recap, copied from Part 3)
Hera turning her back on the bright throne hall and looking down through a break in the cloud (recap, copied from Part 3)
Hera alone in a dark chamber of the palace, fists clenched, a storm of rage breaking over her
Hera on the terrace with a swaddled newborn in her arms, an empty throne beside her
Hera draws back the blanket, sees the child's crooked foot, turns her face away and hurls the bundle off the terrace edge into the clouds
Two sea goddesses rise out of the surf with their arms stretched up to catch the falling baby
A small crooked-legged boy hammering tiny bronze brooches in a sea cave while the pile of jewellery grows year after year and two sea goddesses watch
Hephaestus grown, soot-streaked and grim, looking up from the anvil as if a decision has just been made
The golden throne, finished and gleaming, carried toward Olympus by golden handmaidens
Hera sits on the golden throne and threads of light snap around her arms and waist; she strains and cannot rise
Hephaestus keeps hammering with his back turned on a line of pleading gods at the forge door
A laughing god of wine leads a swaying, drunk Hephaestus up the mountain path toward the glowing summit, where a tiny figure rises free from a golden throne
The forge of Olympus: golden maidens working the bellows and furnaces, new marble houses of the gods rising beyond the arch
Aphrodite, luminous and pearl-white, in a portrait on a sea-bright terrace
A blind poet singing to a lyre in a torchlit king's hall full of listening guests
Ares the god of war, armoured and defiant, a portrait on the terrace
Ares sprinting along the colonnade faster than any other god while Zeus on his throne turns his head away with a scowl
A giant bronze jar lashed with chains on a bleak hillside, two giants dozing on the lid; Hermes lifts the lid and hauls Ares out
Helios's golden chariot blazing across the sky, tilting down toward Olympus, then dropping to the forge door where Hephaestus looks up, turns and strides in
At the anvil, glowing wire drawn finer and finer into chains too thin to see, coiling on the floor
Hephaestus lifting hair-fine chains onto the bedposts and roof beams of the bedchamber, gold glints catching the light
Hephaestus at the house door with a travelling cloak, announcing he is off to Lemnos
Ares sprinting up the path to the house, eyes on the doorway, the moment he sees it is empty
Aphrodite and Ares in the bed under a heavy coverlet, only their heads showing, as the net drops over them and pins them
Hephaestus turning round on the road, hurrying back to his doorway, flinging up an arm to call every god
Hephaestus low-angle at his doorway, the crooked foot turned inward, hand on his chest, looking toward the bed
Zeus enthroned, Hephaestus small before him with an open hand demanding back the heaped bride-gifts
A goddess behind her shutters at dusk, shutting the window and turning away from the sight
Poseidon, Apollo and Hermes striding up the path to the doorway
Apollo leaning toward Hermes with a smirk, nodding at the bed where two heads show under the net
Hermes grinning, spreading both arms wide as if to take on three times the chains
The doorway crowded with gods roaring with laughter, doubled over, one turning to his neighbour to speak
Hephaestus standing by the bed holding the net's chain-end, the whole company laughing around him, Ares red with shame in the bed
Poseidon alone, grave, the only one not laughing, among the blurred laughing gods
Poseidon leaning to Hephaestus with a hand on his shoulder, pleading; Hephaestus unmoved at the net's edge
Hephaestus lifting the net away with both hands and the chains sliding off the lovers
Parchment map of the Aegean: one red line racing north-east to Thrace, one pearl line sailing south-east to Cyprus
A stone altar with a crested bronze helmet and a golden girdle, and between them three small bronze figures: a cowering child, a running child, a girl with a lyre
Camera pulling back from Hephaestus's crooked foot taking a limping step, revealing the golden throne and the net, both traps hung in his forge
Hephaestus alone at his doorway, his big hands opening, glowing chains slipping out of them and drifting away
The empty bed in the grey morning, the net lying loose over it, glints of gold running along its links
The council ring of Olympus with twelve empty thrones, each lighting up in turn with its god's emblem
Three pedestals: a smith's hammer and tongs, a golden girdle, a crested bronze helmet, with the net draped above
End card: poster of the whole story with Hephaestus, Aphrodite and Ares across the frame, title and SUBSCRIBE button
